summary: Presents ways for RSVP routers to start or end RSVP signaling on behalf of a sender or receiver that does not support RSVP. It reviews approaches, how to match reservations to applications, and use cases. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Asking a helper to reserve a table at a restaurant for a friend who can't call, so the booking still happens.

questions: what is an rsvp receiver proxy
what is an rsvp sender proxy
how can rsvp work when the receiver does not support it
subtitle: How a router can make RSVP bandwidth reservations on behalf of a sender or receiver that does not speak RSVP.

tldr.problem: RSVP assumes the data sender and receiver both take part in signaling, yet in many networks the sender, the receiver or both cannot run RSVP although a reservation is still wanted.
tldr.mechanism: An RSVP-capable router acts as a Receiver Proxy (answers Path messages with Resv) or a Sender Proxy (originates Path messages), triggered by Path messages, packet inspection, STUN, an application entity, a policy server or extended RSVP signaling.
tldr.outcome: Reservations can cover the critical part of the path, but the end-to-end RSVP model remains strongly recommended and proxies add configuration and topology constraints.

facts.label: Approaches in Section 4
facts.value: Path, Inspection, STUN, Application_Entity, Policy_Server, RSVP-Signaling triggered

today: RFC 5945 is an Informational RFC published in October 2010, and the unit metadata shows it is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes approaches and says that some of them need extensions defined elsewhere.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs Proxies
sections.content:
Guaranteed quality of service for demanding applications such as voice or video can be achieved by reserving resources in every node on the path. The main IETF protocol for this is the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) from RFC 2205. It does not require every router to support RSVP, but it does assume that both the sender and the receiver do.

RFC 5945 describes how a router can fill in for an endpoint that is not RSVP-capable, so a reservation can still cover part of the path, for example from the sender to the network edge or from edge to edge. The hard part is synchronization: the proxy must work out when a reservation should be set up, kept and torn down, and with what bandwidth, to match what the application needs.

The RFC is clear that the strongly recommended model remains end-to-end RSVP. Proxies bring extra configuration and topological constraints, and end-system RSVP is described as lightweight. The document is meant only for environments where RSVP cannot be used on some endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally both people in a phone call would book the line. A proxy lets one of them be helped by a friendly router when they cannot do the booking themselves.

sections.title: Sender Proxy and Receiver Proxy
sections.content:
In ordinary RSVP the sender emits Path messages and each receiver that wants a reservation answers with a Resv message. A receiver that does not run RSVP silently drops a Path message as an IP packet with an unknown protocol number.

An RSVP Receiver Proxy is an RSVP-capable router that does what the receiver would have done: it sinks the Path message and returns a Resv. RSVP is used upstream of it but not downstream.

An RSVP Sender Proxy is a router that generates Path messages for a sender that is not RSVP-capable and sinks the Resv messages that come back. RSVP is used downstream of it but not upstream. This is harder than the receiver case, because the proxy must build the whole Path message, including the SENDER_TSPEC object, without having received any RSVP message first.

These roles are relative to one unidirectional flow, so a router can be a Receiver Proxy for one flow, a Sender Proxy for another and a regular RSVP router for a third.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver proxy answers the phone for someone who cannot, and a sender proxy places the call for someone who cannot. A single router can do either, depending on the call.

sections.title: Path-Triggered Proxies
sections.content:
In the Path-Triggered Receiver Proxy approach the sender is RSVP-capable and controls synchronization with the application. The proxy treats an arriving Path message as the cue. It establishes Path state, finds the downstream interface, sinks the Path message and behaves as if a Resv had arrived there, which includes admission control, forwarding a Resv upstream, periodic refreshes, and teardown when the Path state is torn down. It may build the FLOWSPEC to mirror the SENDER_TSPEC of the Path.

If admission control fails upstream, a ResvErr reaches the proxy, but ordinary RSVP does not tell the sender. RFC 5946 defines extensions for that notification.

A strict proxy would block an RSVP-capable receiver (or a second proxy) from seeing the Path. To avoid that, the proxy can do dynamic discovery of downstream RSVP functionality: it forwards the Path downstream while also sending the proxy Resv, and if a Resv comes back it converts to an ordinary midpoint router. A drawback is that the sender may briefly see a false reservation. A proxy can also be selective by local policy or by information in the Path message, such as the Application Identity policy element or the Receiver Proxy Control policy element.

The Path-Triggered Sender Proxy for Reverse Direction works the other way round: Path state created by the RSVP-capable endpoint for the reverse direction prompts the proxy to originate Path messages toward that endpoint. It assumes a degree of symmetry in bandwidth and needs no RSVP extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The router waits for the sender to knock, then answers the door for the receiver who is not home. If someone else is home, the router steps aside.

sections.title: Other Ways to Trigger a Proxy
sections.content:
The RFC describes several more triggers.

  • Inspection-Triggered: the proxy watches packets such as SIP or RTSP signaling, or RTCP, and infers when to reserve. It cannot easily tell the application when a reservation fails, so it may mark the DSCP differently for flows that did get a reservation. Encryption and tunneling can defeat it.
  • STUN-Triggered: the proxy uses STUN messages, notably ICE connectivity checks, as the cue. New STUN attributes to carry bandwidth would need to be defined separately and are out of scope.
  • Application_Entity-Controlled: a SIP server or Session Border Controller tells the proxy what to do over a control interface that is out of scope. A variant tunnels Path messages from the application entity to the Sender Proxy using "RSVP over GRE", and another co-locates the entity with the proxy.
  • Policy_Server-Controlled: the same idea, with a policy server between the application entity and the proxy.
  • RSVP-Signaling-Triggered: extended RSVP messages from the capable end request proxy behavior, which would need protocol extensions outside this document.

Section 4.8 also notes that a Receiver Proxy may accept a reservation for a receiver the sender cannot reach, and explains why this is not seen as a significant practical concern.
sections.plainLanguage: There are many ways to tell the helper router when to act: by watching the traffic, by being told by a call manager, or by a special note from the sender.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general security considerations of RFC 2205 apply. RSVP cryptographic authentication (RFC 2747 and RFC 3097) can protect messages hop by hop against corruption, spoofing and replay. Because some RSVP messages use the IP router alert option, RSVP and these proxy approaches are limited to controlled environments.

A proxy acting autonomously inside a router is not seen as a significant new threat, since RSVP already trusts its routers. Proxies controlled by another entity, namely the application-entity and policy-server approaches, add risk: that entity must be trusted and the control interfaces need authentication and confidentiality, which are out of scope. A proxy can even reduce risk, because routers are less exposed to tampering than end systems and the proxy keeps RSVP within one administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the helper router makes promises for others, it must be trusted, and whoever gives it orders must be trusted too.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
Appendix A gives four example environments. In video on demand over broadband aggregation networks, set-top boxes often lack RSVP, so the last IP hop acts as a Path-Triggered Receiver Proxy for admission control; if VoD pumps lack RSVP too, a Session Resource Manager can act as an Application_Entity-Controlled Sender Proxy using RSVP over GRE.

For enterprise WAN voice and video admission control, edge routers act as proxies under control of a SIP server, so the called phone rings only if the reservation across the WAN succeeded. The appendix also covers proxies for mobile access networks and for reservations in the presence of IPsec gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: For example, a video service can have a router near the home check that there is room for a movie before it starts, even though the TV box knows nothing about reservations.
